historical_record.description: A reinforced concrete scenery factory was built for a chain of Market Street picture palaces, designed by O'Brien Brothers and put up by the Lurie Company. One bay runs the full 100-foot depth of the lot as a tower tall enough to hang and paint a full stage drop — its height set by the proscenium of the Granada Theater on Market Street — and the four bays beside it are two storeys of carpentry shop under segmental arches. The tower front carries an arcade of eleven round arches and a bas-relief of nudes with horses.
Built as a four-storey Exotic Revival building designed by the O'Brien Brothers.
Designed by the O'Brien Brothers; the building is listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

For four years the building was the off-site scenery shop for a chain of cinemas that ran mixed programmes of newsreels, orchestral numbers, vaudeville turns and one feature, with staged musical numbers of twenty-five to fifty performers needing elaborate sets. Talking pictures arrived in 1927, features grew longer, vaudeville faded, and the lease ended.

The interior was remodelled for the local branch of the General Cable Company, which stayed until 1934. By 1937 the principal tenant was a building-trade daily, and printing businesses held the building until about 1995 — leaving the scenery platform and the slots for raising and lowering drops in place the whole time.
The four concrete diagonal braces that hold up the north wall of the tower were shaken loose in the earthquake; they have since been reattached.
The Herbert L. Rothschild Building was converted into the Stagehouse Lofts, eighteen units.

The conversion took out the painting platform and the grid that suspended the scenery canvas, though the concrete beams that carried the grid and the piers and haunches that held the platform remain; a third floor clad in vertical corrugated steel was added, set back one bay from the front; and new windows were cut in the tower's north and south walls. The works ran from 1996.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places as the only industrial building in San Francisco identified with a tower built for painting stage scenery.

unknowns: The National Register nomination dates the building to 1924; a South of Market context statement dates it to 1927.
